kept.excerpt: In polling conducted August 24–30, 2026, support was 37.2% for United Russia, 11.6% for the CPRF, 11.5% for New People, 8.7% for the LDPR, and 5.3% for A Just Russia. New People increased by 0.7 percentage points over the preceding week. The release describes a combined telephone and face-to-face methodology, with 1,600 adult respondents and a maximum sampling error of 2.5%.
kept.relevance: The latest verified dated polling release found before the cutoff places New People almost level with the CPRF and ahead of the LDPR, informing its potential seat gains relative to other parties.

kept.excerpt: After the Supreme Court cancelled registration of Yabloko’s State Duma candidate list, social-media posts mentioning the party attracted sharply increased engagement. New People also accumulated reactions rapidly as Russians compared it with Yabloko. At the end of August, parties remaining in the race received free television and radio airtime and space in major print outlets.
kept.relevance: This cutoff-day campaign assessment documents restricted competition and public attention around New People and the excluded Yabloko electorate.

kept.excerpt: In the August 10–16 survey, United Russia received support from 36% of all respondents and 45% of electorally active respondents. Corresponding figures were 11% and 15% for the CPRF, 10% and 12% for New People, 10% and 10% for the LDPR, and 4% and 4% for A Just Russia. Declared intention to participate in the election was 66%.
kept.relevance: The distinction between all respondents and electorally active respondents helps assess turnout effects and the relative positions of New People and its competitors.

kept.excerpt: ExtremeScan’s July survey gave United Russia 24% among all eligible voters, the CPRF 13%, New People 11%, the LDPR 8%, and Yabloko 4%. Two-thirds of respondents named a party they were ready to vote for. Among New People supporters, 69% preferred ending hostilities and reaching a peace agreement to a new mobilization, while 14% preferred mobilization.
kept.relevance: Independent polling provides a comparison with state-pollster estimates and identifies New People’s constituency among voters dissatisfied with wartime conditions.

kept.excerpt: The executive order sets the election of deputies to the State Duma’s new convocation for September 20, 2026. The order enters into force on the day of its official publication. The presidential announcement was published June 16, 2026, at 10:15.
kept.publisher: President of Russia, reproduced unaltered by Public Technologies
kept.relevance: This dated official announcement establishes the scheduled election date for the event covered by Q110.

kept.excerpt: VTsIOM polling showed New People’s support rising from 6.6% to 13.4% over a year, placing it second behind United Russia at 27.7%. The party opposed internet shutdowns and the blocking of messaging applications while avoiding direct attacks on Russia’s leaders and security forces. The analysis describes New People as loyal to the Kremlin and notes its shortage of prominent regional figures.
kept.publisher: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace — Andrey Pertsev
kept.relevance: This analysis explains the source of New People’s earlier polling surge and the political constraints on converting discontent into electoral gains.

kept.excerpt: VTsIOM put New People at 13.4%, while FOM put it at 6%, behind the CPRF at 8% and the LDPR at 10%. In the 2025 local elections discussed in the article, New People fielded 48 candidates for 471 deputy mandates and won one seat. The article describes its Duma faction as three named leading figures plus twelve other members.
kept.relevance: Pollster disagreement, weak local organization, and the reported 15-member faction are important qualifications to both seat projections and the starting-seat baseline.

kept.excerpt: Half of the State Duma’s 450 deputies are elected in single-member constituencies and half through proportional allocation of federal party lists. A 5% threshold applies to the party-list allocation. The analysis states that this electoral formula and the authorities’ control over election administration give United Russia a substantial advantage.
kept.publisher: Institute of Central Europe — Jędrzej Jander
kept.relevance: The mixed electoral system explains why national vote-intention polling alone cannot determine which party will gain the most total seats.

kept.excerpt: CEC chair Ella Pamfilova said United Russia received 324 mandates, the CPRF 57, A Just Russia–For Truth 27, the LDPR 21, and New People 13 following the September 17–19, 2021 election. Rodina, Civic Platform, and the Party of Growth received one seat each, while five mandates went to independent candidates.
kept.publisher: Interfax, reporting the Russian Central Election Commission
kept.relevance: The confirmed previous-election seat distribution supplies a historical baseline for comparing gains across parties, while remaining distinct from subsequent faction membership.

search_notes: Frozen evidence pack for Q110 with publication cutoff 2026-09-07, inclusive. Publication dates were verified from dated source text returned by web_search; the English Carnegie article explicitly states May 11, 2026 despite its /2026/04/ URL. Excerpts are concise factual extracts or English translations/paraphrases. web_fetch failed because of provider configuration, and the requested agent-reach web read fallback returned RATE_LIMITED; no further fallback reads were attempted. Undated live polling dashboards were excluded because fieldwork dates do not establish publication dates. All post-cutoff publications, election outcomes, and prediction-market or betting material were excluded. The 2021 allocation of 13 New People seats and the May 2026 report of a 15-member faction are different measures; a complete immediately pre-election party-seat baseline was not independently verified, so the historical allocation should not automatically be treated as the resolution baseline.
